blocks.text: Long before Lugard drew a map in 1914, people on this land already taxed, judged, raised armies and removed rulers. In Sokoto a man could appeal to an alkali's court; in Oyo the Oyo Mesi could present an empty calabash and end a king's reign; in an Igbo village the same decision might be argued out by titled men and age grades under a tree. Three systems, three answers to the question of who may rule.

blocks.title: Centralised and acephalous systems
blocks.text: A CENTRALISED system has a recognised central authority — a king, emir or oba — with appointed officials and a hierarchy of districts. An ACEPHALOUS (or stateless) system has no single king; power is shared among lineages, age grades, titled men and village assemblies. The Hausa-Fulani emirates, Oyo and Benin were centralised. Most Igbo communities were acephalous.

blocks.markdown:
### The Hausa-Fulani emirate system

After the **Sokoto Jihad** of 1804, led by **Usman dan Fodio**, the Hausa states were reconstituted as emirates under the Sokoto Caliphate. Each **emir** was both political and religious head, ruling in the name of the Sultan of Sokoto and according to **Sharia**.

Administration was hierarchical. The emir appointed **hakimai** (district heads) and village heads to collect tax (including *zakat* and *jangali*), keep order and raise men. Legal disputes went to the **alkali** (Islamic judge). Senior palace officials included the **Waziri** (chief minister), **Madawaki** (commander of the cavalry), **Galadima**, **Sarkin Fada** and others. The system was **theocratic** as well as political: law, tax and legitimacy all flowed from Islam. It was this ready-made hierarchy that later made **indirect rule** relatively easy to apply in the North.

### Oyo and Benin

**Oyo.** The **Alaafin** was king, but not an autocrat. The **Oyo Mesi**, a council of seven hereditary chiefs headed by the **Bashorun**, advised him, checked him, and in the last resort could reject him by presenting an empty calabash (or parrot's eggs), after which custom required the Alaafin to commit suicide. The **Are-Ona-Kakanfo** commanded the army and was required to live outside the capital so that he could not seize the throne easily. The **Ogboni** society provided a further religious and judicial check. Provincial towns were governed by *baales* who owed tribute.

**Benin.** The **Oba of Benin** stood at the centre of a highly centralised kingdom. Palace chiefs and town chiefs, together with the **Uzama** (kingmakers), structured the court. The Oba combined political, ritual and commercial authority more tightly than the Alaafin; checks existed but were weaker than Oyo's famous right of rejection. Guilds organised crafts, and a standing military tradition supported expansion.

items: **Village assembly (ama-ala / oha)** — adult males, and in some communities a wider body, debated and decided local affairs; there was no single king in most Igbo towns.
**Council of elders** — heads of lineages, often the oldest men, who held moral and judicial authority.
**Age grades** — cohorts of men (and sometimes women) of similar age who performed public works, policing, defence and ceremonial duties as they matured.
**Titled men** — *ozo* and similar title-holders who had taken expensive titles and therefore sat with extra prestige in council.
**Oracles and secret societies** — notably the Arochukwu oracle (Ibini Ukpabi), which settled disputes beyond the village and linked communities in a ritual network.
**Exceptions** — some Igbo communities (Onitsha, Nri, Aboh) had kings; examiners still treat 'Igbo village democracy' as the general pattern.

blocks.caption: Three pre-colonial systems compared. Learn the named officials: emir, alkali, hakimi; Alaafin, Oyo Mesi, Are-Ona-Kakanfo, Ogboni; age grades and ozo

blocks.title: Classifying a political system from its officials
blocks.prompt: A passage describes a ruler who is both political and religious head, who appoints district heads called hakimai, and whose judges are called alkali. A second passage describes a village with no king, where age grades police the market and titled men sit with the elders. Classify each system and name one check on power in each.

steps.text: First passage: emir + hakimi + alkali is the Hausa-Fulani emirate — centralised and theocratic. Check on power: the emir was subject to Sharia and to the Sultan of Sokoto; he could in principle be disciplined or replaced within that Islamic hierarchy.

Second passage: no king, age grades, titled men — Igbo village organisation, acephalous. Check on power: open debate in the village assembly, the moral authority of elders, and the ability of age grades to refuse to carry out an unpopular decision.
Do not confuse the second with Oyo. Oyo had a king (the Alaafin) and a named council (Oyo Mesi). Absence of a king is the Igbo clue.
Add a comparative sentence: both systems limited rulers, but one did so through Islamic and hierarchical office, the other through shared village institutions.

blocks.answer: Passage one is the Hausa-Fulani emirate (centralised; checked by Sharia and the Caliphate). Passage two is Igbo village democracy (acephalous; checked by assembly, elders and age grades)

blocks.title: Named officials win marks
blocks.text: Do not write 'the king and his chiefs' for every system. Hausa-Fulani: emir, alkali, hakimi, waziri, madawaki. Oyo: Alaafin, Oyo Mesi, Bashorun, Are-Ona-Kakanfo, Ogboni. Igbo: village assembly, age grades, titled men (ozo), oracles. The empty calabash that could end an Alaafin's reign is the Oyo check examiners love. And never call the Igbo system 'centralised'.

points: Hausa-Fulani emirates after the 1804 jihad were centralised and theocratic: emir, alkali courts, hakimai, and senior officials such as the waziri and madawaki, under the Sokoto Caliphate.
Oyo was a centralised monarchy in which the Alaafin was checked by the Oyo Mesi (headed by the Bashorun), the Are-Ona-Kakanfo and the Ogboni.
Benin was a more tightly centralised kingdom under the Oba, with Uzama kingmakers and palace and town chiefs.
Most Igbo communities were acephalous village republics: assemblies, elders, age grades, titled men and oracles, with no single king.
The useful exam contrast is centralised (Hausa-Fulani, Oyo, Benin) versus acephalous (Igbo), and that contrast later shaped how well indirect rule worked.
